analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare for older and disabled Americans.
analysis.headline: A bill to add dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare was referred to two House committees in June 2016 and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made Medicare pay for dental care (cleanings, fillings, root canals, dentures), vision care (eye exams, glasses, contacts), and hearing care (exams, hearing aids) — services Medicare currently does not cover. Federal payment would have phased in over eight years, reaching 80% of the cost, with limits such as two dental cleanings a year, one pair of eyeglass lenses a year, and one hearing aid per ear every four years. It was never considered by either committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who today pay out of pocket or buy separate private plans for dental, vision, and hearing care — the most common uncovered needs of older Americans. Dentists, eye doctors, audiologists, and hearing aid makers would also gain, because a new federal payment stream would cover services and devices that patients currently skip or pay for themselves.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries needing dental, vision, or hearing care

how_it_helps.text: Adds routine cleanings, exams, fillings, crowns, root canals, extractions, emergency dental care, and dentures to what Medicare covers.
Adds annual routine eye exams, eyeglass lenses and frames, contact lenses (up to a $200 limit per two years), and low-vision devices to Medicare coverage.
Adds hearing exams, audiology services, and hearing aids (one per ear every four years) to Medicare coverage, repealing the current statutory exclusion of hearing aids.

Sets limits to keep costs contained: two cleanings and two exams per year, one denture set per five years, and gives the Health and Human Services Secretary authority to apply further limits or prior authorization.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government and taxpayers, since the bill contains no funding offset for the new benefit. Beneficiaries would also pay: the federal share starts at 0% and rises 10 percentage points a year to 80%, so for the first several years beneficiaries would cover most of the cost themselves, and 20% coinsurance after that.

drawbacks.text: The bill includes no funding mechanism — no tax, premium increase, or offset — so the entire cost of the new benefit would be added to federal deficits or require separate financing.
The federal payment share starts at 0% and climbs only 10 percentage points a year to 80%, meaning that for roughly the first seven years beneficiaries would still pay most of the bill out of pocket.

It gives the Health and Human Services Secretary broad discretion to limit or restructure the coverage, including prior authorization requirements, so the promised benefit could be narrowed after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted at a genuine gap: Medicare covers hospital and doctor care but not the dental, vision, and hearing services older people most commonly need, which they pay for out of pocket or through separate private plans. The design is honest about cost but slow and unfunded — a seven-year phase-in in which patients pay most of the bill, no revenue source, and wide authority for the Secretary to trim the benefit. A serious version would have needed a financing provision and a faster phase-in.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced, then to a health subcommittee, and neither committee ever took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the bill on June 7, 2016, joined by five original cosponsors including John Conyers, Elijah Cummings, and Debbie Dingell.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, and on June 16, 2016 was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
The bill gathered 24 cosponsors, all Democrats, but no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: Medicare beneficiaries continued paying out of pocket or buying separate dental, vision, and hearing coverage from private insurers, and no federal money was committed to the benefit. Providers and insurers selling that coverage outside Medicare kept their market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo: private supplemental insurers and unreformed Medicare

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors, plus the sponsor, were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run committees never acted on it.

industries.note: Dental care would become a covered Medicare service, creating a federal payment stream for cleanings, fillings, root canals, and dentures that patients currently pay for themselves. The benefit phases in slowly, so the revenue build-up would be gradual.

Medicare would cover hearing exams and one hearing aid per ear every four years, converting a mostly out-of-pocket purchase into an insured one. Coverage limits and possible minimum-hearing-loss criteria would restrain volumes.
Routine eye exams, glasses, contacts, and low-vision devices would become covered services, adding covered visits and fittings.

industries.industry: Private supplemental insurers and Medicare Advantage plans selling dental, vision, and hearing riders
industries.note: Millions of beneficiaries buy these benefits today as add-ons priced and packaged by private plans; direct Medicare coverage would replace that product with a cheaper public alternative, shrinking the riders' market.
